qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture eight. Stream processing. This is how events flow from producers to consumers.
A batch job reads three log files, ten thousand lines in all.
A batch job reads three log files.
The input is bounded, so the job reaches the end, finishes, and writes its output.
The input is bounded, so the job finishes.
But posts keep arriving, one after another. This data is unbounded.
But posts keep arriving: the data is unbounded.
There is no last post, so the job waits forever.
The end never comes, so the job waits forever.
Run the batch once a day, and every post waits for midnight.
A daily batch run: every post waits for midnight.
Run it every six hours, and the worst wait shrinks.
Run every 6 hours and the wait shrinks.
Run it every hour, and no post waits more than fifty-four minutes.
Every hour: no post waits more than 54 minutes.
With no windows at all, each post is handled as it arrives. That is stream processing.
No windows at all: each post is handled as it arrives.
A stream is made of events. Here, the user mo seventeen liked post forty-eight twenty-one.
An event: mo_17 liked post 4821.
The event carries a timestamp, the moment it happened.
It carries a timestamp: when it happened.
And it is immutable. Nobody can edit it.
It is immutable: it cannot be edited.
If mo changes their mind, an unlike is added as a new event. Both stay.
A change of mind is a new event.
The phone app is the producer. A consumer uses its events.
A producer makes events; a consumer uses them.
With polling, the consumer asks again and again, and mostly finds nothing.
Polling: the consumer asks again and again.
Every five seconds is seven hundred and twenty checks an hour, for only twelve events.
720 checks an hour find only 12 events.
It is better to be told. A messaging system pushes each event.
Better: a messaging system pushes each event.
And one event can go to many consumers.
One event can go to many consumers.
Now the producer is too fast. It sends six messages a second, and only four are handled.
6 messages a second arrive, but only 4 are handled.
A buffer keeps them all, so the queue just grows.
Buffer: the queue just keeps growing.
Dropping throws away whatever does not fit.
Drop: what does not fit is thrown away.
With backpressure, the producer is told to wait.
Backpressure: the producer must wait.
After ten seconds, twenty wait in the buffer, fourteen are dropped, and fourteen are held back.
After 10 s: 20 waiting, 14 dropped, 14 held back.
Two brokers hold m three and m four in memory.
m3 and m4 wait in the broker's memory.
The lower broker also writes them to disk.
The lower broker also writes them to disk.
Both brokers crash, and memory is wiped.
Both brokers crash: memory is wiped.
After the restart, only the disk copies are left, so the lower one still delivers them.
After the restart, only the disk copies are left.
On top, the producer sends directly. Below, through a broker. Either way, m one reaches both.
m1 goes to A and B either way.
Then consumer B goes offline.
Then consumer B goes offline.
Sent directly, m two and m three are lost to B.
Sent directly, m2 and m3 are lost to B.
The broker kept them, and hands them over when B is back.
The broker kept them and hands them over.
It deletes each message once it is delivered. So consumers can come and go.
With a broker, consumers can come and go.
With load balancing, each message goes to just one consumer.
Load balancing: each message goes to one consumer.
Four messages make four deliveries. The consumers share the work.
4 messages, 4 deliveries: they share the work.
With fan-out, each message goes to every consumer.
Fan-out: each message goes to every consumer.
So the same four messages make eight deliveries.
The same 4 messages: 8 deliveries.
M one goes to consumer two, and m two to consumer one.
m1 goes to Consumer 2, m2 to Consumer 1.
Each sends an ack when it has finished.
Each sends an ack when it is done.
Then m three and m four go out.
Then m3 and m4 go out.
Consumer two crashes, so m three is never acked.
Consumer 2 crashes: no ack for m3.
The broker delivers m three again, to consumer one.
So the broker delivers m3 again.
Consumer one did m four before m three.
Consumer 1 did m4 before m3.
So redelivery can change the order.
Redelivery can change the order.
A batch job ends. A stream never does.
A broker buffers messages, keeps them, and pushes them on.
Without an ack, the message is delivered again.
